description: Small report-quality evaluation set. Rubrics are judged by a human against the saved report and the evidence collected in that run; the workflow's own verification verdict is recorded but is not the rubric outcome.

cases.question: What is the latest stable version of Python?
cases.clarification_reply: Use python.org as the source. Report only the latest stable (not pre-release) version and its release date.

required_answer_points: States one exact latest stable version number (major.minor.patch) in the first body section.
States that version's release date as given by python.org.
Does not present a pre-release (alpha, beta, rc) as the stable version.
acceptable_evidence: python.org Downloads, Source Releases, Windows/macOS release listings or the matching 'Python X.Y.Z' release page.
The Python Developer's Guide status-of-versions page.
output_constraints: Short: a direct answer, no background history or feature tour.
Every body claim cites a source collected in this run.
rubric.honest_gap: Only if no python.org listing was collected: say the latest stable version could not be confirmed from the collected sources and name what was found instead. If a listing with the version and date was collected, labeling the answer INCOMPLETE or refusing to name the version is a failure.
failure_markers: No version number stated as the answer.
Answer labeled INCOMPLETE although the collected listing shows the version and date.
Meta-narration such as 'the provided evidence states' instead of a conclusion.

cases.question: Compare HTTP status codes 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden: what does each mean, and when should a server return one rather than the other?
cases.clarification_reply: Use the HTTP specification (RFC 9110) and MDN. A short comparison is enough.

required_answer_points: 401: the request lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource.
401 responses carry a WWW-Authenticate header with at least one challenge.
403: the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it; supplying (other) credentials will not help, or access is denied for the authenticated client.
A clear rule for choosing: 401 when authentication is missing/invalid and could succeed; 403 when the identity is known (or irrelevant) but not permitted.
acceptable_evidence: MDN Web Docs pages for 401 and 403.
output_constraints: Comparison is easy to scan (short sections or a table).
Every body claim cites a source collected in this run.
rubric.honest_gap: If WWW-Authenticate was not in any collected excerpt, the report should not assert it without a citation; it may omit it and note the gap.
failure_markers: Only defines the codes without the decision rule.
Mentions 'authentication' and 'authorization' without saying which code applies when.

cases.question: For HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests: (1) which RFC defines it, (2) what does it mean, and (3) which response header tells the client how long to wait before retrying?
cases.clarification_reply: Use IETF RFCs and MDN. Answer the three numbered questions directly.

required_answer_points: (2) The user/client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time (rate limiting).
(3) The Retry-After header (optional, MAY be included) indicates how long to wait.
output_constraints: One clearly identifiable answer per numbered subquestion.
Every body claim cites a source collected in this run.
rubric.honest_gap: If RFC 6585 itself was not collected, the report may cite MDN's statement that 429 is defined in RFC 6585, and say the RFC text was not read directly.
failure_markers: Subquestion (2) is answered only by describing the RFC or the header rules, never by stating the meaning (observed in exports/11f6c300-f72a-4371-b393-e5713236592c.md).
Body sentences narrate the evidence ('the provided evidence includes an excerpt...') instead of answering.

cases.kind: genuinely uncertain question / evidence likely missing
cases.question: How many monthly active developers used the LangGraph library in September 2026?
cases.clarification_reply: Any public, citable figure is fine; if there is none, say so and give the closest public proxy metric if one exists.

required_answer_points: States plainly that no authoritative public monthly-active-developer figure for September 2026 was found in the collected sources (unless one was actually collected and cited).
If a proxy (e.g. package downloads, GitHub stars, company-reported usage) is given, it is labeled as a proxy, cited, and not presented as the requested figure.
acceptable_evidence: LangChain/LangGraph official announcements or docs, PyPI statistics pages, GitHub repository pages.
output_constraints: No invented numbers; uncertainty stated in the answer itself, not only in Limitations.
rubric.honest_gap: 'No public monthly-active-developer figure for LangGraph in September 2026 was found in the collected sources; the closest public signal is ... [Sx]' followed by a Limitations entry.
failure_markers: A specific monthly-active-developer number without a source that states exactly that metric.
A long feature overview of LangGraph that never addresses the requested figure.
